# Page 3^page=3
Credit Facilities Amendment Directions, 2026 The RBI has released Credit Facilities Amendment Directions, 2026 for SFBs and Commercial Banks to introduce a new framework for loan against eligible securities and lending to Capital Market Intermediaries The amendments shall come into force from April 1, 2026, or an earlier date when adopted by a bank in entirety.

# Page 4^page=4
Loans against Eligible Securities - Eligible Securities Listed Group-1 equity shares and preference shares; Government Securities, including Treasury Bills and Sovereign Gold Bonds; Listed Debt Securities, including Convertible Debt Securities, rated BBB or higher; Units of Mutual Fund Schemes which are listed or where repurchase/redemption facility is available for such units through the Asset Management Company, with underlying investments in equity, equity related instruments or debt instruments. Units of Exchange Traded Funds (excluding gold, silver and any other commodity ETFs) Units of Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) and Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs);

# Page 5^page=5
Scope: - Loans to individuals, including Hindu Undivided Families (HUFs) which are not commercial entities, shall be covered under this section. Banks may lend to individuals against eligible securities, subject to the LTVs and prudential ceilings specified hereunder. Lending to Individuals LTV shall be monitored on an ongoing basis and a bank shall take steps to rectify the breaches immediately, but in no case later than seven working days from the day of occurrence of such a breach.

# Page 6^page=6
Banks may fix their own prudential limits in terms of their approved policy for loans to individuals against collateral of Government securities (including T-Bills), listed debt securities and units of debt mutual fund schemes. Lending to Individuals - Prudential Ceilings The amount of loan that can be granted to individuals against eligible securities other than those mentioned above shall be capped at ₹1 crore per individual. Within the above limits, loan up to ₹25 lakh per individual may be granted for the purpose of acquisition of securities in secondary markets. If the credit rating of a debt security falls below BBB(-) during the loan period: The borrower must replace the security with an eligible security within 30 working days, or, proportionate portion of the exposure is repaid.

# Page 7^page=7
Banks may grant loans to individuals after ensuring due diligence for subscribing to shares under initial public offer (IPO), follow-on public offer (FPO), or under employee stock option plan (ESOP) upto ₹25 lakh per individual. Provided that the loan amount shall not exceed 75% of the subscription value, i.e., borrowers shall contribute a minimum cash margin of 25%. Lending to Individuals - IPO/FPO/ESOP Financing It shall be ensured that a lien is created on the shares to be allotted under the IPOs/FPOs/ESOPs, and such shares shall be pledged to the lender upon allotment.

# Page 8^page=8
Following loans by a bank shall not be permitted: Loans against its own securities; loans against partly paid shares; loans against securities which are under any lock-in requirements; loans against collateral of Indian Depository Receipts (IDRs); loans against securities of such entities to which banks are not allowed to grant loans and advances; loans to companies for buy-back of shares/ securities loans against Commercial Papers and Non- Convertible Debentures of original or initial maturity upto one year A bank may extend loans to individuals against Long-Term Bonds issued by it for infrastructure financing subject to a ceiling ₹10 lakh per borrower. It is also clarified that a bank shall not extend loans against such bonds issued by other banks. Provided further that, a bank may lend against CDs.

# Page 9^page=9
The LTV ratio given in the table above also applies when bank extend credit facilities to non-Individuals. Banks shall ensure the end use of funds in all such cases is not used for speculative purposes. Lending to non-individuals (other than CMIs) A bank may provide finance, as per its approved policy, to non-financial entities against eligible securities, in addition to other collateral, for financing their working capital or for other productive purposes. A custodian bank may issue Irrevocable Payment Commitments (IPCs) on behalf of their clients, in favour of a Clearing Corporation of a Stock Exchange, subject to meeting any one of the following conditions: 1. Bank has inalienable right over the securities that will be received in settlement. or 2. Transaction must be fully pre-funded i.e., clear funds are available in the customer's account IPC means the bank must pay the clearing corporation without any conditions if settlement obligations arise.

# Page 10^page=10
Irrevocable Payment Commitments (IPCs) A custodian bank may issue Irrevocable Payment Commitments (IPCs) on behalf of their clients, in favour of a Clearing Corporation of a Stock Exchange Issue of an IPC by a bank to the clearing corporation of a stock exchange on behalf of its client is treated as a financial guarantee with a Credit Conversion Factor (CCF) of 100%. CCF for IPC is 100% because an IPC represents a full and unconditional financial guarantee, exposing the bank to the entire committed amount. However, buffer capital is not required to be maintained on the full IPC amount. Capital is required only on the portion that is reckoned as Capital Market Exposure The amount classified as CME will attract a risk weight of 125%, and capital shall be maintained on that risk-weighted amount.

# Page 11^page=11
Credit facilities may be extended only to CMIs which are registered and regulated by a financial sector regulator and are in compliance with the prudential norms prescribed by such regulator. Credit Facilities to Capital Market Intermediaries (CMIs) A bank may provide need-based credit facilities to CMIs to fund their day-to-day operations. In general, all credit facilities to CMIs shall be provided on a fully secured basis (i.e. 100% collateral). A bank may also issue guarantees on behalf of brokers or professional clearing members and in favour of exchanges or clearing houses, as applicable. Such guarantees shall be secured by a minimum collateral of 50%, out of which 25 percent shall be in cash. A bank may extend guarantees for proprietary trading by CMIs subject to the facility being fully secured by collateral of cash, cash equivalents and Government Securities, out of which a minimum 50% shall be cash. If a broker needs a ₹10 lakh margin requirement: Bank issues a guarantee of ₹10 lakh in favor of the Clearing Corporation. Broker must provide at least ₹5 lakh as collateral. Out of ₹5 lakh, at least ₹2.5 lakh must be in cash. A bank shall apply minimum haircut of 40% for equity shares.

Q1. Which of the following can be accepted as eligible securities by banks for granting loans against securities, as per RBI guidelines? 1. Listed Group-1 equity shares 2. Units of commodity Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs) 3. Government Securities including Treasury Bills 4. Listed debt securities rated BBB or above 5. Commercial Papers with original maturity of less than one year A. Only 1, 3 and 4 B. Only 1 and 3 C. Only 2, 3 and 5 D. Only 1, 2 and 4 E. Only 1, 3, 4 and 5 MCQs for Practice
